name: Multi-view projection
text:
# Multi-view projection
Also called: Multi-view rasterization, Orthographic voxelization, 3-pass voxelization

## Overview
Multi-view projection generates a volumetric representation of a 3D mesh by rasterizing the geometry from multiple distinct viewpoints, typically aligned with the principal axes of the scene's bounding box. It solves the problem of occlusion and grazing-angle artifacts inherent in single-view projection methods by ensuring every surface element is visible from at least one viewpoint, thereby preventing "shadow" voxels [S1, S2, unofficial]. It differs from [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md) by using multiple views to cover all surface normals, and from [GPU Voxelization via Compute Shaders](2549-gpu-voxelization-via-compute-shaders.md) by relying on standard rasterization pipelines rather than explicit ray-casting or compute-based intersection tests.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of decomposing 3D occupancy into a set of 2D rasterization passes. The shared mathematical and procedural steps are:

1.  **Bounding Box Definition:** Define an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing the scene geometry, with min $(bb_{min})$ and max $(bb_{max})$ coordinates. The voxel grid resolution $R = (R_x, R_y, R_z)$ maps world coordinates to discrete indices.
2.  **View Direction Selection:** Select a set of orthogonal view directions. The standard configuration uses three directions aligned with the principal axes: $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ [S1, S2, unofficial].
3.  **Camera Setup:** For each view direction $A \in \{X, Y, Z\}$, construct an orthographic camera.
    *   **Position:** The camera is positioned at $bb_{max} + \delta \cdot \mathbf{u}_A$, where $\mathbf{u}_A$ is the unit vector of axis $A$ and $\delta$ is a small offset (e.g., $0.2$ units) to ensure the frustum fully encompasses the bounding box [S1].
    *   **Projection:** An orthographic projection matrix is used. The frustum width/height is set to $1.02 \times \text{range}_A$ (where $\text{range}_A = bb_{max,A} - bb_{min,A}$) to provide a margin [S1].
    *   **Near/Far Planes:** The near plane is set to a small positive value (e.g., $0.1$), and the far plane is set to $1.2 \times \text{range}_A + \delta$ to cover the entire depth extent [S1].
4.  **Rasterization:** Render the triangle mesh from each camera. Depth testing is typically disabled or configured to allow overwriting to ensure all intersected voxels are marked, as the goal is occupancy rather than surface visibility [S1].
5.  **Voxel Mapping:** Fragment positions in clip space are transformed into voxel grid indices. A [scaling matrix](#4126-scaling-matrix-construction.md) $S = (R_x/\text{range}_x, R_y/\text{range}_y, R_z/\text{range}_z)$ and translation based on $bb_{min}$ map continuous coordinates to discrete integer indices $(i, j, k)$ [S1].
6.  **Atomic Write:** Occupied voxels are written to a 3D texture or buffer. [Atomic operations](#3684-atomic-operations-for-global-counters.md) are required if multiple fragments or passes write to the same voxel location concurrently [G].

## Subtopics

### [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md)
This method produces a 6-separating (tunnel-free) [voxelization](#12-voxelization.md) of a planar triangle using only a single 2D projection along the dominant axis of the triangle's normal vector. It leverages the "thinness" property of voxelization to avoid the multiple projections required by sibling methods like [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md) or [3-Pass Voxelization](5300-3-pass-voxelization.md). By projecting along the normal's dominant axis, the algorithm ensures that every pixel whose center lies within the projected triangle yields a unique voxel in the corresponding column, while edge cases are resolved via crosshair-segment intersection tests. Choose this method for simple planar primitives where computational efficiency is critical and the geometry is not complex or highly curved.

### [Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md)
[Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization](#3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md) rasterizes scene geometry into a 3D texture or a compressed 2D "worksheet" representation using three orthographic cameras aligned with the principal axes of the scene's bounding box. It solves the problem of generating a volumetric representation for subsequent volume rendering (such as [cone tracing](#5679-cone-tracing.md)) by ensuring every surface element is visible from at least one viewpoint, thereby preventing "shadow" voxels caused by occlusion or grazing angles. It differs from [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md) by using three views to cover all surface normals, and from [3-Pass Voxelization](5300-3-pass-voxelization.md) by typically performing the synthesis in a single GPU-driven pass or via efficient 2D-to-3D transcoding rather than explicit CPU-side merging of three separate 3D volumes. Choose this method when high-quality, gap-free voxelization is required for real-time rendering pipelines.

### [3-Pass Voxelization](5300-3-pass-voxelization.md)
[3-Pass Voxelization](#5300-3-pass-voxelization.md) is a rasterization-based technique that eliminates cracks and missing data in the voxel grid by rendering the scene from three orthogonal directions, one for each principal axis (X, Y, Z). Unlike single-view projection methods which suffer from occlusion shadows and geometric distortion, this approach ensures that every surface element is visible from at least one viewpoint, guaranteeing complete voxel occupancy. It is chosen when geometric completeness is critical and the computational cost of three render passes per object is acceptable.

### [Volumetric Representation via Depth Map Registration](6435-volumetric-representation-via-depth-map-registration.md)
This method constructs a 3D volumetric representation from a sparse set of calibrated multi-view images by registering estimated depth maps into a voxel grid. It specifically addresses non-Lambertian scenes by using individual minimum cost per view for depth estimation rather than a global threshold, and represents geometry as a sparse voxel cloud where voxel values indicate the number of views mapping to that location. It distinguishes itself from static voxelization methods by incorporating an iterative refinement loop that cleans scattering voxels, smooths sharp corners, and re-evaluates visibility to ensure the final volume accurately represents the real scene for virtual view synthesis. Choose this method for multi-view stereo reconstruction from image sequences rather than mesh inputs.

### Multi-View Stereo Cost Volume Construction
#### definition
A cost volume $V_c$ is constructed from feature volumes $\{Vf_i\}$ of $N$ reference views to perceive coarse scene structure and provide [scene priors](#1413-regularization-losses.md) for sampling, skipping blank areas [S1].
#### parameter
$L$: Number of depth layers in the cost volume. Typical value: 16 [S1].
#### pitfall
Checkerboard artifacts caused by deconvolution layers in the Res-Unet processing the cost volume are eliminated by replacing deconvolution with combinations of upsampling and convolution layers [S1].

## Background
Multi-view projection techniques have evolved from early voxelization methods for ray tracing [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) structures to modern real-time rendering pipelines. The 3-pass approach is a standard technique for generating voxel cones for cone-traced global illumination [S1, S2, unofficial]. The worksheet synthesis method was developed to address hardware limitations in rendering directly to 3D textures on consumer PC platforms, offering a memory-efficient alternative [S2, unofficial]. In the context of [Neural Radiance Fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) ([NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md)), multi-view stereo cost volumes are used to provide [depth priors](#8727-depth-and-geometry-supervision.md) for efficient scene reconstruction, as seen in methods like [NeRF-SDP](#8554-nerf-sdp.md) [S1].
